title: Lakshmana's warning
hook: an apology, a flood of armies, and an embrace
carry: I may have slipped, who doesn't

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tara met Lakshmana's anger with calm and honesty, and this time somebody listened.

Lakshmana walks into the inner palace. It's beautiful, full of gardens, music and fine things, and Valmiki describes it in detail, maybe so we'll feel how far Sugriva has drifted from a cave on a mountain. Sugriva is on his throne, in fine clothes and garlands, his queens around him. He sees Lakshmana and gets to his feet. Now the king of the monkeys has to face the brother of the man who made him king.
screen: `THE INNER PALACE.` → `SUGRIVA ON HIS THRONE.` → `HE GETS TO HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana speaks hard words. A king who takes help and doesn't keep his promise is ungrateful, he says, and for ingratitude there's no atonement. He repeats Rama's message. Sugriva doesn't argue. Everything I have, he says, I owe to Rama. I may have slipped. Who doesn't? But I'm his friend and his servant, and I'll follow him with my whole army. If I've failed through carelessness or overconfidence, forgive me. A good apology owns the fault, doesn't drown in it, and moves to action. Sugriva does all three, and Lakshmana softens at once. You've spoken well, he says. Come and see Rama. Sugriva rides out with Lakshmana to Rama, gets down, and bows with joined palms. Rama receives him with an embrace and asks him to sit beside him. And while they talk, the armies arrive. Valmiki turns it into a parade: monkeys and bears pour in past counting, from mountains and seashores, from forests and snowy peaks, until they seem to cover the earth. The Sanskrit word for forgiveness, kshama, also means patience, and it's also a name for the earth, the one who bears everything. Rama doesn't hold the lost weeks against him. The friendship is back where it was, and stronger, because now it has been tested and repaired. And Rama turns to the real question: where do we look first?
screen: `NO ATONEMENT FOR INGRATITUDE.` · `SUGRIVA: FORGIVE ME.` · `AN EMBRACE, AND ARMIES.` · `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS, THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Think of a small fault of yours that someone might still be holding, and own it privately and plainly: yes, I did that. Breathe out, and let yourself also be someone who can be forgiven. Then think of someone you could forgive, and let your hand rest open on your knee, palm up.
Lakshmana's warning. It ends in Sugriva's apology, a flood of armies, and Rama's embrace.
Your line: I may have slipped, who doesn't. A fault owned, and a friend back at his side. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Kshama, forgiveness or forbearance, is listed among the virtues in Hindu texts such as the Bhagavad Gita (16.3), and the reconciliation of Rama and Sugriva is told as an example of friendship repaired.

original.note: Sanskrit kṣamā: forgiveness, patience, forbearance; also a name for the earth, who bears everything.

what a scholar hears: Lakshmana's words on ingratitude are in Kishkindha 34; Sugriva's apology in Kishkindha 36; the armies and Rama's embrace in Kishkindha 37–39.

kshama.meaning: forgiveness and patience; also a name for the earth

Sugriva.meaning: the monkey king, Vali's younger brother, Rama's ally

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, beside him in exile

Rama.meaning: the exiled prince of Ayodhya, the Ramayana's hero
